summary:
ASTRO-ACE is a real-time medical monitoring system for astronauts. It combines a smart ring, a suit with nine sensors and an onboard lab with ACE-MED, a clinical agent that assesses five areas every minute: the immune system, bone health, cardiovascular health, mental health and life support. It compares every reading with reference ranges from hospitals, medical societies and NASA standards. When it detects a risk, it shows the evidence, recommends the right countermeasure and, during life-support emergencies, acts on its own. A 3D digital twin of the crew member, modeled in Blender, reacts in orbit, aboard the space station or on the Moon, and the 3D Body module shows the effect on each organ. Everything is stored in PostgreSQL for the flight surgeon.

The project addresses the challenge of protecting crew health on long missions, when communication delays with Earth prevent immediate care. It matters because it catches early the problems that today are only found after the return, and it gives medical autonomy to missions to the Moon and Mars.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

ASTRO-ACE is the system we built to monitor astronaut health throughout a mission. The crew member wears a smart ring and a suit with nine sensors. The ring measures pulse, heart rate variability, oxygen saturation, temperature and movement, and it also has a dosimeter and an emergency button. The suit records the ECG, blood pressure, core temperature, breathing, helmet CO₂ and oxygen, suit pressure, stress level, bone loading and an immune panel. Everything is sent from an ESP32 over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi to our server, which delivers it in real time to the crew console and to mission control.

At the heart of the system is ACE-MED, our medical agent. Every minute it reviews five areas that deteriorate in space: the immune system, bones, heart, mental health and life support. It compares each reading with reference values from hospitals, medical societies and NASA standards. When something goes out of range, it explains what it found, what points to it and what to do. In an emergency, such as a suit leak or an oxygen drop, it acts without waiting for a response from Earth.

To make the crew member’s condition clear at a glance, we built a 3D astronaut in Blender. The model reacts with its body: it puts a hand to its chest during an arrhythmia, shivers with a fever and struggles for air with hypoxia. It can be shown in orbit, aboard the space station or walking on the Moon. We also added a body map that shows what is happening in the heart, lungs, brain and skeleton. Every reading and every decision is saved for the flight surgeon.

What are the benefits?

Today many health problems in space are found during scheduled checkups or only after the astronaut returns. With ASTRO-ACE, an arrhythmia, a fever or a drop in oxygen is caught within the first minute. Bone loss and heart deconditioning, which develop slowly, are visible from day one. The crew member doesn’t have to stop working to take measurements, and the medical team gets every alert with its evidence. The system also lets the crew practice medical emergencies without real risk.

What is the expected impact?

We want ASTRO-ACE to give medical autonomy to long missions, such as those in the Artemis program and, in the future, missions to Mars, where communication with Earth can take up to 20 minutes. We also see uses on Earth: workers on oil platforms, in mines or at polar bases, and patients in rural communities with little access to a doctor.

What tools did we use?

The web app is built with JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with Three.js for the 3D scenes and Web Bluetooth to connect the ring. The server runs on Node.js and Express, and the data is stored in PostgreSQL. The 3D body module uses React with React Three Fiber. We modeled and animated the astronaut and the ring in Blender using Python scripts. The firmware is written in C++ for the ESP32, and the app is deployed on Railway, with the code on GitHub. We based the medical thresholds on NASA’s Human Research Program, the NASA-STD-3001 standard, the Canadian Space Agency’s Bio-Monitor and TBone studies, and ESA research.

What makes it creative?

Instead of a separate device for each measurement, we brought the ring, the suit and the lab together into one system that works as a whole. We liked the idea of the 3D astronaut “telling” how it feels through its body, not just through numbers on a screen. We also wanted the agent to always explain where each conclusion comes from, because in medicine trust depends on that.

What factors did we consider?

Crew safety came first. That’s why the system only acts on its own during life-support emergencies, and clinical decisions always stay with the flight surgeon. We made sure every threshold had a reliable source and that the model reflected real conditions: microgravity, radiation, lunar gravity and communication delays. We also wanted the interface to be clear for both the astronaut and mission control, to use low-cost hardware, and to document everything in Spanish and English.
